author: Ahmed Ibrahim
title: Holocaust Centre Condemns Tamihere's Nazi Germany Comparison
text:
Past comparisons, especially to nazism, risk trivializing genuine concerns about fascism, possibly leading to public apathy when real threats emerge.
Using Nazi comparisons in political debate can desensitize the public, making future warnings about fascism ineffective.
- Political discourse is increasingly using Nazi comparisons, raising concerns about their impact.
- Experts warn that overusing such analogies can dilute the gravity of genuine fascist threats.
- The Holocaust Centre has previously commented on similar comparisons made in political speeches.
- Politicians are urged to exercise extreme caution with historical comparisons in public debate.
The escalating use of Nazi comparisons in political discussions is a growing concern, potentially undermining legitimate accusations of fascism.
“If we were ever faced with a regime that actually was fascist, the call to alert would fall on deaf ears as it would be easy to dismiss,” stated one observer.
Criticism of political figures
During a recent podcast, Te Pāti Māori president John Tamihere referred to Tama Potaka, the National’s Māori Development spokesperson, as “a disgrace” for his stance on co-governance policies. Tamihere also labeled National minister Judith Collins as “ugly.” Collins declined to comment on the remark. Potaka had not yet responded to a request for comment.
Tamihere has stated his intention to contest the Kelston seat, currently held by Labour deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni, in 2026.
There was no immediate response from Tamihere to a request for comment.
Explanation of Changes & how Questions are Answered:
Why: The article addresses the growing concern over the increasing use of Nazi comparisons in political discourse and the potential for these comparisons to diminish the impact of genuine warnings about fascism. Who: Key figures involved are John Tamihere (Te Pāti Māori president), Judith Collins (National minister), Tama Potaka (National’s Māori Development spokesperson), Winston Peters (New Zealand First leader), and Carmel Sepuloni (Labour deputy leader). Experts at Victoria University of Wellington and the Holocaust Centre are also referenced.
